title: Greatest Books: Page Turners
description: 60 questions on the books the world keeps reading: famous first lines, who wrote what, unforgettable characters, where the stories happen, classics from Japan to Nigeria to Colombia, and how the books first reached print.

questions.question: Which novel opens with the words "Call me Ishmael"?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.explanation: Herman Melville's narrator introduces himself with three words before setting out on the whaler Pequod (1851).

questions.question: Which novel begins "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife"?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen's 1813 novel opens with this ironic line, which sets up the Bennet family's marriage plans.

questions.question: Which Charles Dickens novel opens "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times"?
questions.explanation: A Tale of Two Cities (1859), set in London and Paris around the French Revolution, opens with this famous run of contrasts.

questions.question: Which novel begins "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way"?
questions.explanation: Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina (1878) opens with this line, often quoted as the "Anna Karenina principle."

questions.question: Which novel opens with Colonel Aureliano Buendía, facing a firing squad, remembering the afternoon his father took him to discover ice?
options: Love in the Time of Cholera
questions.explanation: Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 masterpiece opens with this line, which moves across decades in a single sentence.

questions.question: Which novel begins "It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen"?
questions.explanation: George Orwell's 1949 novel signals from its first sentence that something is wrong with Winston Smith's world.

questions.question: Which book opens "In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit"?
options: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
questions.explanation: J. R. R. Tolkien said he scribbled the line on a blank page of an exam paper he was marking; The Hobbit followed in 1937.

questions.question: Which story begins "All children, except one, grow up"?
questions.explanation: It is the first line of J. M. Barrie's novel Peter and Wendy (1911), the book version of his play Peter Pan.

questions.question: Which novel opens with its narrator unsure whether his mother died "today" or "yesterday"?
questions.explanation: Albert Camus's The Stranger (L'Étranger, 1942) begins with Meursault's flat report of his mother's death.

questions.question: In which story does Gregor Samsa wake from uneasy dreams to find himself transformed into a gigantic insect?
questions.explanation: Franz Kafka's novella The Metamorphosis (1915) begins with the transformation and never explains it.

questions.question: Who wrote Don Quixote?
questions.explanation: Miguel de Cervantes published Don Quixote in two parts; it is often called the first modern novel.

questions.question: Who wrote Things Fall Apart (1958)?
questions.explanation: The Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart, one of the most widely read African novels.

questions.question: Who wrote Beloved, winner of the 1988 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?
questions.explanation: Toni Morrison wrote Beloved (1987) and later won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993.

questions.question: Who wrote Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus?
questions.explanation: Mary Shelley was 20 when Frankenstein was published, anonymously, in 1818.

questions.question: Which poet wrote The Divine Comedy, with its journey through Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso?
questions.explanation: Dante wrote it in the early 14th century. Virgil appears in the poem as his guide, but did not write it.

questions.question: Who wrote Madame Bovary?
questions.explanation: Flaubert was put on trial for obscenity after it was serialized in 1856, was acquitted, and saw the book become a classic.

questions.question: Who wrote Mrs Dalloway (1925), which follows one day in a London hostess's life?
questions.explanation: Virginia Woolf's novel follows Clarissa Dalloway as she prepares for a party on a single June day.

questions.question: Who wrote Midnight's Children, winner of the 1981 Booker Prize?
questions.explanation: Salman Rushdie's novel follows children born at the moment of India's independence; it later won the Booker of Bookers.

questions.question: Who wrote The Master and Margarita, in which the Devil visits Soviet Moscow?
questions.explanation: Bulgakov worked on it until his death in 1940; it was first published, censored, in 1966–67.

questions.question: Who wrote The Great Gatsby (1925)?
questions.explanation: F. Scott Fitzgerald's Jazz Age novel follows the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby on Long Island.

questions.question: In Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, what is the name of Scout's lawyer father?
questions.explanation: Atticus Finch defends Tom Robinson in court; Jem is Scout's brother and Boo Radley the reclusive neighbor.

questions.question: What is the name of Don Quixote's loyal squire?
questions.explanation: Sancho Panza rides a donkey beside the knight. Rocinante is Don Quixote's horse and Dulcinea his imagined lady.

questions.question: Which Jules Verne character commands the submarine Nautilus?
questions.explanation: Captain Nemo appears in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas (1870). Phileas Fogg is Verne's round-the-world traveler.

questions.question: Who is the impoverished former student at the center of Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment?
questions.explanation: Raskolnikov drives the 1866 novel. Myshkin is from The Idiot, Ivan from The Brothers Karamazov, Pierre from War and Peace.

questions.question: Who narrates The Great Gatsby?
questions.explanation: Nick Carraway, Daisy Buchanan's cousin, rents the house next to Gatsby's and tells the story.

questions.question: Who is Sherlock Holmes's great criminal adversary, called "the Napoleon of crime"?
questions.explanation: Arthur Conan Doyle introduced Professor James Moriarty in "The Final Problem" (1893).

questions.question: In Little Women, which March sister is the aspiring writer?
questions.explanation: Louisa May Alcott based Jo March, who writes stories and plays, partly on herself.

questions.question: In Wuthering Heights, which brooding foundling is taken in by the Earnshaw family?
questions.explanation: Mr. Earnshaw brings Heathcliff home from Liverpool in Emily Brontë's 1847 novel. Rochester belongs to her sister Charlotte's Jane Eyre.

questions.question: In Homer's Odyssey, who waits faithfully in Ithaca for Odysseus to come home?
questions.explanation: Penelope holds off her suitors for years, famously unweaving each night the shroud she weaves by day.

questions.question: In Victor Hugo's Les Misérables, which police inspector relentlessly pursues Jean Valjean?
questions.explanation: Inspector Javert hunts the former convict Valjean for years; Thénardier is the scheming innkeeper.

questions.question: James Joyce's Ulysses follows Leopold Bloom through a single day in which city?
questions.explanation: The novel takes place in Dublin on 16 June 1904, a date fans now celebrate as Bloomsday.

questions.question: What is the name of the fictional town founded by the Buendía family in One Hundred Years of Solitude?
questions.explanation: Macondo is García Márquez's town. Comala is from Juan Rulfo's Pedro Páramo and Yoknapatawpha is Faulkner's county.

questions.question: Thomas Hardy set Tess of the d'Urbervilles and his other major novels in which semi-fictional region of England?
questions.explanation: Hardy revived the old Anglo-Saxon kingdom name Wessex for his south-west England. Barsetshire is Anthony Trollope's county.

questions.question: In Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner, Amir and Hassan grow up together in which country?
questions.explanation: The boys fly kites together in 1970s Kabul; the adult Amir later returns to Afghanistan from California.

questions.question: In John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath, the Joad family leaves Oklahoma for which state?
questions.explanation: Driven off their farm during the Dust Bowl, the Joads head west along Route 66 to look for work in California.

questions.question: In Thomas Mann's The Magic Mountain, Hans Castorp stays at a sanatorium in which Swiss resort?
questions.explanation: Castorp goes to Davos to visit his cousin for three weeks and stays seven years.

questions.question: Victor Hugo's The Hunchback of Notre-Dame is set in which city?
questions.explanation: The novel is set in 15th-century Paris around the cathedral, and helped spark efforts to preserve it.

questions.question: Orhan Pamuk's murder mystery My Name Is Red is set among miniature painters in which city?
questions.explanation: The novel is set in Ottoman Istanbul in the late 16th century. Pamuk won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2006.

questions.question: In Bram Stoker's Dracula, Jonathan Harker travels to the Count's castle in which region?
questions.explanation: Harker, a young English solicitor, journeys to Transylvania to finalize the Count's purchase of a house in England.

questions.question: In which present-day country is Things Fall Apart set?
questions.explanation: The novel follows Okonkwo in the Igbo village of Umuofia in what is now south-eastern Nigeria.

questions.question: The Tale of Genji, often called one of the world's first novels, was written about 1,000 years ago in which country?
questions.explanation: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court, wrote it in the early 11th century.

questions.question: In One Thousand and One Nights, who tells stories each night to delay her execution?
questions.explanation: Scheherazade leaves each tale unfinished at dawn so that King Shahryar spares her for another night.

questions.question: Which mischievous hero escorts the monk Tang Sanzang in the Chinese classic Journey to the West?
questions.explanation: Sun Wukong is the star of the 16th-century novel; Guan Yu belongs to Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

questions.question: The Epic of Gilgamesh, among the oldest surviving works of literature, comes from which ancient civilization?
questions.explanation: It survives on clay tablets written in cuneiform, telling of a king of the Sumerian city of Uruk.

questions.question: Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace is set against which conflict?
questions.explanation: The novel spans 1805 to 1812 and beyond, including Napoleon's invasion of Russia.

questions.question: In Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince, the narrator is a pilot stranded in which desert?
questions.explanation: Saint-Exupéry was a pilot himself and had crashed in the Sahara in 1935, years before the book appeared in 1943.

questions.question: The Bhagavad Gita forms part of which Sanskrit epic?
questions.explanation: The Gita is a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and Krishna on the eve of the Kurukshetra war in the Mahabharata.

questions.question: In Goethe's Faust, the restless scholar makes a pact with which devil?
questions.explanation: Mephistopheles strikes the bargain for Faust's soul; Goethe published Part One in 1808.

questions.question: Rabindranath Tagore, the first non-European winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature (1913), wrote chiefly in which language?
questions.explanation: Tagore wrote in Bengali and translated some of his poems, including Gitanjali, into English himself.

questions.question: Who became the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1988?
questions.explanation: The Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz is best known for his Cairo Trilogy.

questions.question: Most of Charles Dickens's novels first reached readers in what form?
questions.explanation: Dickens published most of his novels in weekly or monthly parts, building suspense from one installment to the next.

questions.question: Frankenstein began as an entry in a ghost-story challenge proposed by which poet in 1816?
questions.explanation: At the Villa Diodati near Geneva, Byron suggested that each guest write a ghost story; Mary Shelley's became Frankenstein.

questions.question: The Victorian novelist "George Eliot," author of Middlemarch, was really which writer?
questions.explanation: Mary Ann Evans chose a male pen name, partly so that her fiction would be judged on its own terms.

questions.question: Under which pen name did Charlotte Brontë first publish Jane Eyre in 1847?
questions.explanation: The three sisters published as Currer (Charlotte), Ellis (Emily) and Acton (Anne) Bell.

questions.question: Which Russian author's novel Doctor Zhivago was first published in Italy in 1957 after being refused at home?
questions.explanation: The Milan publisher Feltrinelli brought it out in Italian. Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1958 but was forced to decline it.

questions.question: Kafka's The Trial was published after his death because which friend ignored his request to burn his papers?
questions.explanation: Max Brod, Kafka's friend and literary executor, published The Trial in 1925 and later The Castle and Amerika.

questions.question: In which century was the first part of Don Quixote published?
questions.explanation: Part One appeared in Madrid in 1605 and Part Two in 1615, the year before Cervantes died.

questions.question: James Joyce's Ulysses was first published as a book in 1922 by the Shakespeare and Company bookshop in which city?
questions.explanation: Sylvia Beach published it from her Paris bookshop on 2 February 1922, Joyce's 40th birthday.

questions.question: J. R. R. Tolkien wrote The Hobbit while he was a professor at which university?
questions.explanation: Tolkien was a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford from 1925, and The Hobbit grew from stories he told his children.

questions.question: Where did Arthur Conan Doyle stage Sherlock Holmes's apparent death in "The Final Problem" (1893)?
questions.explanation: Holmes and Moriarty go over the Swiss falls together. Public outcry helped bring Holmes back a decade later.

editorialNotes: Widely acknowledged classics across eras and cultures (about a third from outside the English-language canon). Opening lines quoted in their standard English translations. Plot details limited to premises and famous, long-public turns. Difficulty is editorial. All explanations are original paraphrases.
